explain.body: Organization starts with atoms and becomes more complex at each level: molecules, organelles, cells, tissues, organs, organ systems, and organisms.

explain.title: Cells and tissues
explain.body: A cell is the smallest unit with characteristics of life. A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to perform one or more specific functions.

explain.title: Organs and organ systems
explain.body: An organ is made of related tissues working together. An organ system consists of multiple organs working together to perform related functions.

explain.title: Emergent properties
explain.body: When parts interact at a higher level, they can create functions that the separate parts cannot perform alone. For example, different heart tissues work together so the heart can pump blood.

explain.title: Examples in plants and animals

explain.body: An organ is made of tissues that work together for a particular function. The textbook defines an organ system this way: “An organ system consists of organs that work together to perform essential functions.” In plants, the two main systems are the root system and the shoot system.

explain.title: A leaf is a complex organ
explain.body: The textbook states: “In plants, leaf is a complex organ made of various related tissues.” Epidermal tissue forms the outer layer. Mesophyll tissue lies between the two epidermises and is the site of photosynthesis. Vascular tissue contains xylem and phloem.

writtenQuestions.text: Describe the tissue composition of the stomach. How does each tissue contribute to the digestive function of the stomach?
modelAnswer: The inner wall of the stomach is made up of glandular epithelial tissue.
It secretes mucus, which protects the inner wall from acid, and gastric juice containing pepsinogen and hydrochloric acid.
Connective tissue lies beneath the epithelial tissue; it provides structural support and contains blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatics.
There are three smooth muscle layers: outer longitudinal, middle circular, and inner oblique.
These muscles contract and relax to mix food with gastric juice.
The outer connective tissue encircles and supports the stomach.

explain.title: The stomach is made of tissues
explain.body: “Stomach is an important organ of the digestive system. It is responsible for the partial digestion of proteins. It also stores food.” Its epithelial tissue secretes mucus and gastric juice; connective tissue provides support; and smooth muscle layers mix food with gastric juice.

writtenQuestions.text: What is homeostasis, and why is it important for organisms?
modelAnswer: Homeostasis is the ability of an organism to maintain a stable internal environment despite changes in the external environment.
It is important because cells function properly only when conditions such as temperature, pH, and the concentrations of salts, glucose and oxygen are kept in the normal range.

writtenQuestions.text: How does the human body maintain a stable internal temperature?
modelAnswer: When body temperature rises above normal, the temperature-regulating centre in the brain sends a message to sweat glands.
Sweating occurs and, as sweat evaporates, heat is lost and body temperature falls towards normal.
When body temperature falls, the centre sends a message to muscles, causing shivering.
Shivering generates heat and raises body temperature towards normal.

explain.title: What homeostasis means
explain.body: Homeostasis is defined as the ability of an organism to maintain a stable internal environment of the body despite changes in the external environment. Temperature, blood pressure, blood sugar and pH are examples of conditions the body regulates.

explain.title: Why homeostasis matters
explain.body: Cells work properly only when conditions around them, such as temperature, pH, and the concentrations of salts, glucose and oxygen, stay in the normal range.

explain.title: Temperature responses
explain.body: When body temperature rises, sweating causes heat loss as sweat evaporates. When temperature falls, shivering generates heat. Both responses help bring body temperature towards normal.

explain.title: Systems work together
explain.body: Several organ systems help maintain homeostasis. The nervous and endocrine systems coordinate activities; the respiratory system supplies oxygen and expels carbon dioxide; and the cardiovascular system helps regulate temperature and pH while carrying necessary substances to cells.

explain.title: Other system roles
explain.body: The digestive system distributes nutrients to cells. The urinary system eliminates wastes and regulates water and salt balance. The integumentary system protects the body and helps regulate temperature through sweating.

example.question: Q5.9. Define homeostasis and explain its importance. Discuss how different organ systems work together to maintain homeostasis.
example.answer: Homeostasis is the maintenance of stable internal conditions in an organism. It is important because cells and organs need suitable conditions to function properly. Different organ systems work together: the digestive system supplies nutrients, the respiratory system supplies oxygen, the circulatory system transports materials, and the excretory system removes wastes. Their coordinated actions help maintain stable internal conditions.

explain.title: Organisation from small to large
explain.body: The order is cell → tissue → organ → organ system. Cells with similar functions form tissues; different tissues work together in organs; organs cooperate in organ systems.

explain.title: Tissues perform specialised jobs
explain.body: Animal tissues include epithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous tissues. Plant tissues include epidermal tissue, mesophyll, xylem, and phloem. Their structures suit their functions.

explain.title: The stomach digests food
explain.body: Stomach epithelial tissue produces mucus, pepsinogen, and hydrochloric acid. Connective tissue supports the stomach and contains blood vessels and nerves. Smooth muscle churns food and mixes it with digestive juices.

explain.title: The leaf captures and transports materials
explain.body: Palisade mesophyll carries out most photosynthesis; spongy mesophyll has air spaces for gas exchange. Xylem brings water to the leaf, phloem carries food, and the epidermis protects the leaf.

explain.title: Organs and systems cooperate
explain.body: Plant roots anchor and absorb water and minerals, while shoot organs support photosynthesis, transport, and reproduction. In humans, organ systems cooperate to provide needed materials and remove wastes.

explain.title: Homeostasis keeps conditions stable
explain.body: Homeostasis means maintaining stable internal conditions. Systems such as the respiratory, circulatory, digestive, and excretory systems work together so cells and organs can function properly.

mistakes: Reversing the order of tissue and organ in the organisation hierarchy.
Saying xylem transports food or phloem transports water; xylem transports water and minerals, while phloem transports food.
Confusing palisade and spongy mesophyll: palisade mainly carries out photosynthesis, while spongy mesophyll has air spaces for gas exchange.
Listing stomach tissues without explaining what each does.
Defining homeostasis without explaining why it matters or how organ systems help maintain it.
Describing only one side of a comparison question instead of giving a difference between both terms.

notes.title: Levels of organization
notes.answer: The levels from simplest to most complex are atom, molecule, organelle, cell, tissue, organ, organ system, and organism.
notes.explanation: Living things are organized from small, simple parts to larger, more complex levels. Parts at each level work together, so higher levels can do things their separate parts cannot do alone.
notes.simple: Small parts join together to make bigger parts. When the parts work together, the bigger structure can do more.
examples: Muscle cells work together to form muscle tissue, which can contract and generate force.
Different tissues in the heart work together so the heart can pump blood.
steps: Atoms combine to form molecules.
Molecules combine to form organelles.
Organelles work together in cells.
Similar cells form tissues.
Related tissues form organs.
Organs work together in organ systems.
Organ systems together make an organism.

notes.title: Plant organs and organ systems
notes.answer: Plants have a root system and a shoot system. The root system anchors the plant and absorbs water and salts; the shoot system includes stems, branches, leaves, and flowers and enables processes such as photosynthesis and reproduction.
notes.explanation: A plant organ is made of tissues that work together. Plant organs also work together in two main systems: the root system and the shoot system.
notes.simple: Roots work mostly below the ground. Stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits make up the shoot system, mostly above the ground.
examples: A leaf is an organ: its tissues work together in photosynthesis, gas exchange, and transport.
Roots anchor a plant and absorb water and minerals; the stem supports other organs and transports materials.

notes.checkAnswer: The root system anchors the plant and absorbs water and minerals; the shoot system includes stems, branches, leaves, and flowers.

notes.title: Human Organs and Organ Systems
notes.explanation: The stomach is an organ made of different tissues. Its epithelial tissue secretes mucus and gastric juice, while its smooth muscle layers contract and relax to mix food with gastric juice. Organ systems are groups of organs that work together to perform important body functions.
notes.simple: An organ is made of tissues working together. An organ system is made of organs working together.
examples: The stomach is an organ in the digestive system.
The respiratory system includes the lungs, trachea, and bronchi.

notes.checkAnswer: The epithelial tissue secretes mucus and gastric juice, and the smooth muscles mix food with gastric juice.

notes.title: Homeostasis: keeping the body's conditions stable
notes.answer: Homeostasis is the ability of an organism to maintain a stable internal environment of the body despite changes in the external environment.
notes.explanation: Homeostasis keeps the conditions inside the body stable enough for cells and organs to work properly. The body responds to changes, such as a rise in temperature or blood glucose, and brings conditions back towards normal.
notes.simple: Homeostasis is the body's way of keeping its inside conditions steady, even when things change outside or inside the body.
examples: When body temperature rises, sweat evaporates from the skin and heat is lost.
When blood glucose rises after drinking juice, insulin lowers it towards normal.
steps: A change occurs, such as body temperature rising above normal.
The body detects the change and sends signals to the organs that can respond.
Sweat glands secrete sweat.
As sweat evaporates, heat is lost and body temperature falls towards normal.
notes.checkQuestion: What happens when body temperature rises above normal?
notes.checkAnswer: Sweating helps lose heat, so body temperature falls towards normal.

notes.title: How living things are organised
notes.explanation: A multicellular organism is organised in levels, from cells to organ systems. Different tissues and organs work together, and organ systems cooperate to keep the organism alive and its internal conditions stable.
notes.simple: Small parts join together in an organised way. Cells make tissues, tissues make organs, and organs work together in organ systems.
examples: In a stomach, epithelial tissue produces secretions, while smooth muscle mixes food.
In a leaf, mesophyll carries out photosynthesis, while xylem transports water.

written.text: Q5.9. Define homeostasis and explain its importance. Discuss how different organ systems work together to maintain homeostasis.
modelAnswer: Homeostasis is the maintenance of stable internal conditions in an organism.
It is important because cells and organs need suitable conditions to function properly.
Different organ systems work together to maintain homeostasis.
The digestive system supplies nutrients, the respiratory system supplies oxygen, and the circulatory system transports materials around the body.
The excretory system removes wastes, helping keep the internal conditions stable.

written.text: Q5.10. Describe how the respiratory and circulatory systems work together to maintain homeostasis of oxygen and carbon dioxide levels in the body.
modelAnswer: The respiratory system brings oxygen into the lungs, where it passes into the blood.
The circulatory system carries oxygen in the blood to body cells.
Carbon dioxide from the cells passes into the blood and is carried to the lungs.
The respiratory system removes the carbon dioxide, helping maintain suitable oxygen and carbon dioxide levels in the body.

written.text: Q5.1. How does the structure of epithelial tissue relate to its function in different parts of the body?
modelAnswer: Epithelial tissue is made of closely arranged cells that form sheets covering body surfaces and lining organs.
This arrangement provides a protective covering.
Depending on its location, epithelial tissue can also absorb substances or secrete them.
For example, stomach epithelial tissue secretes mucus, pepsinogen, and hydrochloric acid.

written.text: Q5.2. Evaluate the importance of organ systems working in harmony and predict the consequences of a failure in one system on the others.
modelAnswer: Organ systems work in harmony because each depends on the others to carry out the body's life functions.
Together, they supply and transport useful materials, remove wastes, and maintain homeostasis.
If one system fails, other systems may not receive the oxygen, nutrients, or materials they need.
Wastes may also build up if the system responsible for their removal is not working.
As a result, the function of other systems and the whole body may be disrupted.
